summary: The Israel-Hamas war has put Egypt back in the spotlight as a regional powerbroker, which could win it Western economic support while it struggles with its worst economic outlook in decades. Israel and the US reportedly hope Egypt will temporarily house Gazan refugees in exchange for incentives, but President El-Sisi has rejected the idea, and analysts see domestic and regional factors ruling out a deal. Economists still expect Egypt to get backing as 'too big to fail', including a possible IMF program increase to over $5 billion.
one_line: Egypt, in economic crisis and seen as too big to fail, is courted by the West but refuses to take in Gaza refugees.
key_facts: Israel has spoken to counterparts in several countries about Egypt temporarily housing Palestinians fleeing Gaza, possibly in UN- and US-funded tent camps in the Sinai Peninsula, to be returned once military operations end; it is unclear if Israel put this directly to Egypt.

President Abdel-Fattah El-Sisi faces elections in less than two months and has rejected any suggestion that Egypt host Gazan refugees, suggesting Israel take Palestinians into its Negev desert instead.
Egypt reached a deal with the IMF in December and is in talks to boost the rescue program to over $5 billion from $3 billion.
Riccardo Fabiani of Crisis Group said the IMF's key shareholders in the US and Europe may pressure the lender to soften requirements despite Cairo's slow pace of reforms.
Egypt already hosts some 9 million refugees and other migrants from countries including Syria, Sudan, Yemen and Libya.
Opening a route for Palestinians could create a new security risk in the Sinai peninsula, where the army has only just gained a handle on its fight with Islamist militants.
Robert Satloff of The Washington Institute said Egypt's political leadership considers refugee acceptance a red line and would prefer worsening financial distress.
In 1991 Egypt secured forgiveness of half of its $20.2 billion debt owed to the US and allies in exchange for supporting the anti-Iraq coalition in the Gulf war.
Egypt was the second-largest source of manpower in the US-led coalition in 1991, so Satloff said it couldn't expect a similar level of aid today.
El-Sisi hosted a 'Summit for Peace' in Cairo on Saturday with Middle East and European leaders; Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman was absent.
Egypt led the 1973 attack on Israel that triggered the Yom Kippur war, then signed a peace treaty and established full diplomatic relations with Israel in 1980.
Strategists suggest Egypt could offer Saudi Arabia a role co-leading the Palestinian issue for the Arab world in return for financial support.
